matches.blind_hypothesis: Prodigies reported at Rome before Trasimene
matches.note: Prodigy wave recovered from Orosius, but the institutional outcome (senate-decreed expiations, lectisternium, perpetual Saturnalia) is lost.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Flaminius set out against the auspices, ignoring adverse omens
matches.note: The auspice violation survives (periocha + Florus), but the GT event is the senate's political dispute over the legitimacy of his magistracy ('two consuls created, but one'), which no witness preserves.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Public mourning at Rome on Trasimene news; two mothers died of joy
matches.note: The two-mothers vignette is straight from Livy 22.7; the forum concourse is the same event.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Ver sacrum vowed on the authority of the Sibylline books
matches.note: Matched; the constitutional nuance (pontifex's ruling that it required an order of the people) is lost but the event is the same.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Q. Fabius Maximus appointed dictator and sent against Hannibal
matches.note: Matched, but every witness lineage flattens the unprecedented PRO-dictatorship created by popular vote into an ordinary dictatorship; the reconstructor correctly noted that no witness states the appointment procedure.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Minucius obtained by order of the people an imperium equal to the dictator's
matches.note: Matched; the tribune Metilius, his bill, and Varro's lone senatorial support are lost, but the popular enactment itself survives in the periocha.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Minucius equal imperium (army divided in consequence)
matches.note: The reconstructor folded 'diuisoque exercitu' into the equalization event rather than coding Fabius's refusal of alternate-day command as a separate decision; granularity loss, not content loss.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Minucius voluntarily resubmitted, saluting Fabius as father
matches.note: Matched including the key legal point that the restoration was by voluntary act, not law.

matches.blind_hypothesis: New consuls Aemilius Paulus and Terentius Varro succeeded Fabius
matches.note: Only the succession outcome survives; the single-consul return and the nobles pressing Paulus on Varro are lost. The reconstructor correctly declined to invent an election narrative.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Post-Cannae plan to abandon Italy suppressed by Scipio at sword-point
matches.note: Matched; Orosius even preserves Caecilius Metellus as instigator, agreeing with Livy 22.53 against the periocha's anonymous 'nobiles adulescentes'.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Panic and mourning gripped Rome after Cannae
matches.note: The panic survives as a bare summary; Fabius's emergency program (confining women, silencing lamentation, gate guards, news control) is entirely lost.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Eight thousand slaves armed and enrolled
matches.note: Matched across all four witnesses, figure and 'quod numquam ante' novelty intact; the volunteer-consent inquiry survives only in Orosius.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Senate refused to ransom the Cannae prisoners
matches.note: Matched with the senate's reasoning preserved in Eutropius; Torquatus's speech and the oath-evader's surrender are lost.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Dictator 'Decimus Iunius' appointed, emergency levy from age seventeen
matches.note: This IS Book 22 content (Livy 22.57: M. Junius Pera, levy from seventeen, four legions) despite the prompt-worthy suspicion; Orosius's praenomen 'Decimus' is a witness error for Marcus, and the senatorial authority for the appointment is lost, but the event matches.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Vestals Opimia and Florentia condemned for incestum
matches.note: Matched; periocha's 'Florentia' for Floronia is a minor corruption. The live burial, Floronia's suicide, and the scourging of Cantilius are lost.

matches.blind_hypothesis: Varro met by a crowd and thanked for not despairing of the republic
matches.note: Matched, formal public act and rationale both preserved.

blind_only.hypothesis: Dictator Iunius enrolled men liable for crimes or debts with promised impunity, about six thousand
blind_only.note: This is Livy 23.14 (Junius Pera's edict freeing capital criminals and judgment debtors, ~6,000 men), i.e. Book 23 / late 216. Witness-caused: Orosius narrates the Junius dictatorship continuously across the book boundary with no seam. The reconstructor's medium confidence did not flag the boundary risk.

blind_only.hypothesis: Arms taken from temples and private wealth poured into the empty treasury
blind_only.note: Two-way misplacement: the temple arms are the Gallic spoils of Livy 23.14 (Book 23), and the private-wealth contribution is Livy 26.36 under Laevinus (210 BC, Book 26). Witness-caused by Florus's anachronistic recovery montage and Orosius's compression; the reconstructor explicitly flagged Florus's 'Laevino Marcelloque consulibus' but still admitted the event.

blind_only.hypothesis: Younger citizens sought elders' advice in electing consuls
blind_only.note: This is Livy 26.22 (the junior Veturian century consulting the seniors in the election for 210 BC, Book 26). Witness-caused: Florus's undated recovery passage; the reconstructor flagged it as possibly belonging to a later book and rated it low confidence, so it is a self-aware misplacement.

ground_truth_only.note: The irregular extension of the levy to sons of freedmen left no trace in any witness.
The army's insubordinate preference for Minucius is absorbed into the Minucius-vs-Fabius arc; no witness preserves it as camp insubordination.
Fabius selling his farm after the senate withheld silver for his prisoner exchange — a senate-procedure story no epitomator kept.
Twenty-five slaves crucified for conspiracy in the Campus Martius; wholly lost.
The auspically flawed dictatorship of Veturius Philo (forced abdication, interregnum) vanished from all witnesses — procedural constitutional law dies first.
The violent patrician-plebeian contest and Herennius's tribunician agitation behind Varro's election are gone; witnesses record only the resulting consuls.
The conversion of the soldiers' voluntary compact into a legally compulsory oath ('which had never before been the case') left no witness trace despite being an explicit Livian first.
The pre-Cannae camp sedition over Hannibal's feigned retreat is absent.

Eutropius preserves the deadlock ('inpatientia Varronis consulis contradicente altero consule'); the reconstructor cited it in the consular-succession event's notes but did not code the command deadlock as its own event — a granularity miss on attested content.
The senate's thirty-day limit on mourning to restart the rites of Ceres is lost; witnesses keep the mourning, not the decree.
The live burial of Gallic and Greek couples and the Delphi embassy of Fabius Pictor are absent from all four witnesses — striking, since it is the most sensational religious act in the book.
Carthalo's dismissal by the dictator's lictor is gone; Eutropius keeps only the generalized 'nemo pacis mentionem habere dignatus est'.

Eutropius 3.11 explicitly attests 'multae Italiae civitates... se ad Hannibalem transtulerunt'; the reconstructor did not code it, perhaps reading it as external/military rather than domestic-political content.

metrics.notes: Recall = (11 full + 5 partial x 0.5) / 29 = 13.5/29 = 0.466. Precision = 15 of 18 blind events match real Book 22 content = 0.833; the 3 misses are all cross-book leakage (Books 23 and 26), all witness-caused, two of three explicitly flagged as risky by the reconstructor. 16 of 29 GT events were touched via 15 blind events (one blind event maps to two GT events); 13 GT events were lost entirely, 11 of them absent from all witnesses.

qualitative: What survives epitomization is the memorable and the unprecedented: dictatorships, the Minucius imperium-equalization and its reversal, the Vestal scandal, the ver sacrum, the slave enrollment ('quod numquam ante'), the ransom refusal, and emotive vignettes like the mothers dead of joy and the thanks to Varro — 11 of 16 recovered events are full matches. What dies is procedural politics: the flawed Veturius dictatorship and interregnum, the violent Varro election contest, the senate's silver dispute with Fabius, the mourning-limit decree, the military-oath legalization, and the freedmen-sons levy all vanished from every witness, so elections, vetoes, and senate procedure are structurally unrecoverable, while even the sensational human sacrifice was dropped by all four lineages. The main false-confidence pattern is not witness agreement but witness continuity: Orosius's seamless narrative pulled the Book 23 debtor levy into Book 22, and Florus's undated recovery montage injected Book 26 material (private wealth to the treasury, the juniors deferring to seniors) — though the reconstructor flagged both Florus risks. Conversely, the scorer's own trap inverted: Orosius's 'Decimus Iunius' dictatorship is genuine Book 22 content (Livy 22.57, M. Junius Pera) with only the praenomen corrupted, showing that single-witness oddities can be right. The two reconstructor-side misses were both demotions of attested content to footnotes: the Cannae command deadlock and the Italian defections sat in Eutropius's text but were never coded as events.
